We'll take a project that lives only on your computer and give it a full
version history and an online home, using three tools, each with one
clear job:

| Tool               | Its job                                     |
|---------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| **Positron**       | Build your local commit history              |
| **GitHub Desktop** | The bridge — publish and sync, no SSH setup   |
| **GitHub.com**     | The remote — host and view your project online|

Everything through the GitHub Desktop step happens **locally** on your
own computer. After that, we connect the local project to GitHub. A
collaboration workflow (fork & pull requests), the command-line
equivalent of everything we do visually, and institutional hosting
options are all covered later, in Extending Further.

## Why Version Control?

You've probably seen a folder like this:

```
analysis.R
analysis_v2.R
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_FINAL.R
analysis_final_FINAL_really.R
```

This is version control done by hand — and it's painful. You can't
remember what changed between versions, you can't safely delete any of
them, and collaborating means emailing files back and forth.

**Git** solves this. It's a **time machine for your project**: it saves
snapshots (called **commits**) of your work over time, so you can always
see what changed, when, and why — and roll back if you need to. Instead
of five copies of a file, you keep **one** file with a complete history.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Git vs. GitHub
- **Git** is the tool that tracks changes on your computer (local).
- **GitHub** is a website that hosts git projects online (remote), so
  you can back them up and share them.

You can use git entirely on its own. GitHub adds the online home.
:::

## Checking Whether Git Is Initialized

Before using Positron's Source Control tab, confirm git is actually
tracking your project. Open the **Terminal** tab in Positron — because
you're working inside an R project, it opens directly in your project
folder.

```bash
git status
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Git is ready

```
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/
        scripts/
        ...
```

Your repository is already initialized. Move on to the next section.

### Not a git repository

```
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
```

Run one command to fix it:

```bash
git init
```

You should see:

```
Initialized empty Git repository in /path/to/your/project/.git/
```

Run `git status` again — you should now see the "Git is ready" output.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Why the Terminal First?
Positron's Source Control tab is a visual interface built on top of the
same git commands you just ran. Starting here lets you see what's
happening under the hood before switching to the GUI — and `git init` is
the one thing the GUI can't do for you.
:::

## Local Git in Positron: Modify → Stage → Commit

Your control center for git in Positron is the **Source Control** tab in
the left activity bar. Every change you save to your history goes
through three steps:

1. **Modify** — you edit files in your project as usual
2. **Stage** — you pick which changes to include in the next snapshot
3. **Commit** — you save those staged changes as a permanent snapshot

The "stage" step is what surprises newcomers: git lets you choose
*exactly* what goes into each commit, so you can group related changes
together instead of dumping everything at once.

When you change files, they appear in the panel with a letter:

| Indicator | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| **U** | Untracked — a new file git doesn't know about yet |
| **M** | Modified — an existing file has changed |
| **A** | Added — a new file that's been staged, ready to commit |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Two Zones
The panel has two areas: **Changes** (modified but not yet staged) and
**Staged Changes** (packed and ready to commit). Clicking the **+** next
to a file moves it from Changes → Staged Changes.
:::

### Your First Commit

1. **Look at the Source Control tab.** You should see several files
   listed as untracked (**U**) — the scripts and data files you've
   worked with so far.
2. **Stage everything.** Hover over the **Changes** heading and click
   the **+** icon to stage all files at once. They move into
   **Staged Changes**.
3. **Write a commit message.** In the message box, type something
   descriptive: `Add project scripts and data`.
4. **Commit.** Click the **✓ Commit** button.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Write Messages for Your Future Self
A good commit message finishes the sentence "This commit will…".
`Add data loading script` is useful; `stuff` and `update` are not.
:::

### A Second Commit

1. **Make an edit.** Open any script and add a comment line at the top:

   ```r
   # Analysis script — tracked with git
   ```

2. **Check the panel.** The file now shows an **M** (modified) under
   **Changes**.
3. **Review the diff (recommended).** Click the filename to open a diff
   view — additions in green, deletions in red. Reviewing the diff
   before committing is the single best habit for catching mistakes
   early.
4. **Stage and commit.** Click **+**, type `Add header comment to
   analysis script`, and click **✓ Commit**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — A Peek Behind the Curtain
The Source Control panel just runs git commands for you. In the
**Terminal**, run:

```bash
git status
git log --oneline
```

You'll see the current state and the commits you just made. You never
*have* to use the terminal — but it's good to know the GUI isn't doing
anything magic. The full command-line workflow is in Extending Further.
:::

## Excluding Data Files: The `.gitignore` File

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Don't Store Large Data Files in Git
Git is built for *code and text*, not big datasets — it keeps every
version of every file, so a 100 MB dataset can balloon your repo after a
few edits, GitHub enforces a 100 MB per-file limit, and git compresses
text well but handles large binary data poorly.

But the 100 MB limit is a technical ceiling, not a research-data
strategy — even a file that fits comfortably under it usually still
doesn't belong in a code repository. If it's your raw data or your
processed data, it needs to be preserved in a **data repository**: a
system built for depositing, citing, and sharing research data —
Zenodo, OSF, Figshare, or an institutional repository — which is a
fundamentally different kind of place than a GitHub repo. [Arc 8](modules/arc_8.qmd)
covers packaging and depositing your data for exactly this reason.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Where Should Data Live Instead?
| Data Size | Recommended Approach |
|-----------|----------------------|
| Small reference data (< 10 MB) | OK to include if it rarely changes |
| Medium (10 MB–1 GB) | Cloud storage (Dropbox, Drive, OneDrive) — document the location |
| Large (> 1 GB) | Institutional repositories, OSF, Zenodo, Figshare |
| Very large | **Git LFS** — stores big files externally, keeps references in git |
:::

You already have a `.gitignore` in your project root — `renv::init()`
created it back in Arc 1 to exclude its package cache. Extend it:

1. **Open it.** In Positron's Explorer pane, click `.gitignore` in your
   project root. (If you don't see it: **View → Show Hidden Files**.)
2. **Add these lines** below what's already there:

   ```gitignore
   # Ignore data folders
   raw_data/
   processed_data/

   # Ignore large output files
   outputs/*.pdf
   outputs/*.html
   ```

3. **Save the file.**
4. **Watch git react.** The files in `raw_data/` and `processed_data/`
   disappear from the Source Control panel — git is now ignoring them.
5. **Commit the updated `.gitignore`**, with the message
   `Extend .gitignore to exclude data files`.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Track Code, Not Data
Keep your repository lean by tracking **code, not data**. This is
exactly what the Arc 2 "data management gone awry" story was missing:
note where your data actually lives in your README instead of
committing it directly.
:::

## Publishing to GitHub with GitHub Desktop

Your project now has a local history. Let's give it an online home so
it's backed up and shareable. **GitHub Desktop** handles authentication
through your browser — no SSH keys, no tokens.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Make Sure You Have These First
- A free [GitHub account](https://github.com/signup)
- [GitHub Desktop](https://desktop.github.com/) installed and signed in
:::

**Step 1: Sign in to GitHub Desktop**

1. Open **GitHub Desktop**.
2. Go to **File → Options → Accounts** (macOS: **GitHub Desktop →
   Settings → Accounts**).
3. Click **Sign in** next to GitHub.com. Your browser opens — approve
   the request, and you're authenticated.

**Step 2: Add your existing project**

1. **File → Add Local Repository**.
2. Navigate to your project folder and select it.
3. Click **Add Repository**.

GitHub Desktop now shows your project and its full commit history — the
same commits you made in Positron.

**Step 3: Publish**

1. Click **Publish repository** at the top.
2. Confirm the name and add a short description if you like.
3. **Keep this code private** — leave this checked for research work
   (uncheck it only if you intend the project to be public).
4. Click **Publish repository**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Positron ↔ GitHub Desktop
Keep editing and committing in **Positron**, then switch to
**GitHub Desktop** and click **Push origin** to send your latest commits
to GitHub. Push whenever you want your online copy up to date.
:::

## Seeing It on GitHub.com

1. Go to [github.com](https://github.com) and open **Your repositories**.
2. Click the repository you just published.

You should see all your files, and — by clicking the **commits** link
(or the clock/history icon) — the complete history you built in
Positron. Your local project now has an online backup.

**Local-first vs. remote-first.** There are two ways a project's life
can begin:

- **Local-first (what we just did):** you start on your own computer,
  build a history, then publish to GitHub — like writing a document on
  your desktop and later uploading it to share.
- **Remote-first (cloning):** the project already exists on GitHub. You
  **clone** it — downloading a complete copy, history and all — before
  you start working, like a colleague sharing a document you download
  to edit.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — When You'll Use Remote-First
You'll use the remote-first / clone workflow when collaborating on
someone else's repository — covered in Extending Further, below.
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** initialized and confirmed a git repository, practiced
the modify → stage → commit cycle twice (once reviewing a diff), extended
`.gitignore` to keep data out of version control, and published the
result to GitHub with GitHub Desktop — giving the project both a local
history and an online home.

**Why it matters:** your commit history is becoming a lab notebook for
your code — a record of what changed and why, that exists independent of
your memory. You can now read the U/M/A status indicators, explain why
large data files don't belong in git, and tell local-first apart from
remote-first — the foundation every collaboration workflow below builds
on.

## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — Collaborating with Fork & Pull Requests
One of the most powerful aspects of version control is **collaboration**.
This walks through a complete, real-world workflow where one person
proposes a change to another person's project.

**Roles:** the **Project Owner** owns the original repository and
decides what changes to accept; the **Contributor** wants to suggest
improvements, fixes, or additions.

**The workflow:** Fork → Clone → Branch → Edit → Push → Pull Request.

**Fork the repository.** On GitHub.com, navigate to the owner's
repository and click **Fork** — this creates an exact copy of the entire
project history, all commits, branches, and files, under your own
account. You can experiment freely without affecting the original.

**Clone your fork.** Click the green **<> Code** button, copy the HTTPS
URL, then in GitHub Desktop: **File → Clone Repository**, paste the URL,
choose a save location, and click **Clone**.

**Create a new branch.** In GitHub Desktop, open the **Current Branch**
dropdown → **New Branch**. Give it a descriptive, lowercase,
hyphen-separated, verb-focused name (`add-readme-documentation`, not
`new-feature` or `MyBranch`), then **Create Branch** → **Publish branch**.

**Make your edits in Positron.** Click **Open in Positron** from GitHub
Desktop, make your change (a new file, a fix, documentation), and save.

**Commit and push.** Back in GitHub Desktop, review your changes by
clicking each filename, write a descriptive commit message, click
**Commit to [your-branch-name]**, then **Push origin**.

**Open a pull request.** After pushing, click **Create Pull Request**.
Give it a clear title and a description explaining what changed and why:

```
## Summary
Added comprehensive README documentation to help users understand
the project's structure, objectives, and prerequisites.

## Changes Made
- Created README.md in the project root
- Documented setup and prerequisites

## Why This Improvement
The repository lacked documentation explaining what it covers and
what participants need to get started.
```

**The owner's review.** On the original repository's **Pull requests**
tab, open the PR, review line-by-line differences under **Files
changed** (green = additions, red = deletions), leave comments, and
either **Approve and Merge**, **Request Changes**, or **Close without
Merging**.

- **Be constructive** — focus on the code, not the person
- **Be specific** — point to exact lines and suggest improvements
- **Be appreciative** — thank contributors for their time
- **Test locally** — for important changes, pull the branch and test it
  yourself before merging

**After merging,** the owner can safely delete the contributor's branch;
the contributor switches back to `main`, pulls the latest changes, and
deletes their own feature branch — their contribution is now part of the
official project history.

**Why this matters:** the original project is never at risk during
development, every change goes through review before integration,
contributors and maintainers can discuss openly, and every contribution
is documented with clear attribution.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — Git on the Command Line
The Positron Source Control panel is a visual interface that runs git
commands for you in the background. Here's how to run those same
commands yourself — useful for speed, advanced operations, and remote
servers where no GUI is available.

```bash
git status
```

```bash
git add .
```

`.` means "add all changed files in the current directory and
subdirectories." To stage a single file, name it:
`git add scripts/analysis.R`.

```bash
git commit -m "Describe what changed"
```

```bash
git log --oneline
```

Confirm your data files are actually excluded after adding a
`.gitignore`:

```bash
git status --ignored
```

You should see your data folders listed under "Ignored files."

If you've set up SSH (just below) or an HTTPS credential, you can
connect and push from the terminal instead of GitHub Desktop:

```bash
git remote add origin git@github.com:username/yourreponame.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

| Approach | Best For |
|----------|----------|
| GUI (Source Control panel / GitHub Desktop) | Visual learners, reviewing diffs, getting started |
| CLI (Terminal) | Speed, advanced operations, remote servers |

Many experienced users mix both: GUI for reviewing diffs, CLI for quick
commits. On Windows, you may see "CRLF will be replaced by LF the next
time Git touches it" — this is normal, git converting Windows-style line
endings to Unix-style for consistency, and safe to ignore.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — SSH Key Authentication (Advanced)
GitHub Desktop handles authentication for you, so you don't need this
for the core workflow. But if you prefer to push from the **command
line**, SSH keys let you authenticate securely without typing a password
every time.

PATs (personal access tokens) are an HTTPS-based alternative, but they
expire every 90 days and need renewal. **SSH is preferred for long-term
research projects** because it's a one-time setup — if SSH is blocked by
your network, GitHub Desktop (HTTPS) is the reliable fallback.

**Check for existing keys** in the Positron Terminal:

```bash
ls ~/.ssh
```

If you see `id_ed25519` or `id_rsa`, you already have keys — skip to
adding your key to GitHub, below. Otherwise:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## macOS / Linux

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
```

Press **Enter** to accept the default save location, and again twice to
skip a passphrase (optional).

```bash
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

## Windows

These commands work in the **Positron Terminal** or **Git Bash**
(installed with Git for Windows) — the Positron Terminal is recommended
for consistency.

```bash
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"
```

Press **Enter** to accept the default save location, and again twice to
skip a passphrase (optional).

```bash
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | clip
```

If `clip` doesn't work, run `cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub` and copy the output
manually. If `ssh-agent` won't start, try running Positron or Git Bash
**as Administrator** — and if you see "Could not open a connection to
your authentication agent," run `ssh-agent bash` first, then retry
`ssh-add`.

:::

The `.pub` file is your **public key** — safe to share with GitHub. The
file without `.pub` is your **private key** — never share this. If
someone asks for your SSH key, they always mean the public one.

**Add it to GitHub:** profile photo → **Settings** → **SSH and GPG
keys** → **New SSH key** → give it a descriptive title (`My Positron
Laptop`) → paste the key → **Add SSH key**.

**Test the connection:**

```bash
ssh -T git@github.com
```

Type `yes` if prompted about authenticity. You should see:
`Hi username! You've successfully authenticated...`
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — GitHub Enterprise Options at Yale
If you're working with sensitive research data, Yale offers two GitHub
Enterprise options beyond standard GitHub.com.

**GitHub Enterprise Server (On-Premises)** — a self-hosted platform
running within Yale's secure infrastructure. Suitable for
version-controlling analysis scripts, maintaining reproducible research
pipelines, and integrating with Yale's research computing resources.
Hosted on Yale's own infrastructure; supports **High** data
classification (including HIPAA-covered data); full control over data
location and security policies.

**GitHub Enterprise Cloud** — adds advanced functionality to GitHub.com,
including SAML single sign-on with Yale credentials, additional GitHub
Actions minutes, and enhanced security/compliance features. Cloud-based,
managed by GitHub; supports **Moderate** data classification (not
suitable for high-sensitivity data).

| Platform | Best For |
|----------|----------|
| GitHub.com | Public research, open-source projects, teaching |
| GitHub Enterprise Cloud | Collaborative research with Yale auth, moderate-sensitivity data |
| GitHub Enterprise Server | High-sensitivity data, HIPAA compliance, institutional governance |

Contact [Yale ITS](https://its.yale.edu/) for access, or
[request GitHub Enterprise support via Yale ServiceNow](https://yale.service-now.com/it?id=service_offering&sys_id=bc29b84997f88a506f0430671153af28).
:::
